newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia miners criticise gold royalty plan.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia miners criticise gold royalty plan.

text.p: Australia's largest gold producing state, Western Australia, has come under criticism by miners opposing a government proposal to impose a gold royalty.

Western Australia state premier Richard Court has said the state's proposal was to introduce a royalty of 1.25 percent of gold sale proceeds from January 1 next year, rising to 2.5 per cent by July 1999, to compensate for cuts in Federal funding
Western Australia produces about 70 percent of Australia's nearly 300 tonnes of gold each year and a gold royalty is seen adding tens of millions of dollars in revenues to the state.

"It is most important that the government take full account of the net costs of a gold tax to the state, and its impact on the state's biggest export industry," Peter Lalor, chairman of the Chamber of Minerals and Energy Gold Forum, said in a statement
The Association of Mining and Exploration Companies (AMEC) has commissioned an economic study on what impact a gold royalty would have on the mining industry.
"AMEC has not taken this (the royalty proposal) as a fait accompli," George Savell, the organisation's chief executive officer, told Reuters.
Unlike miners in other states, gold miners in Western Australia currently are exempt from paying royalties on gold although other metals are subject to royalties in that state.

Queensland has a 2.75 percent gross royalty, while in New South Wales a net smelter levy of four percent is equal to about a two percent gross royalty. The Northern Territory has an 18 percent net profit royalty.
But this year, Western Australia is facing a potential loss of around A$33 million in Federal funds and the state is looking at ways to offset the shortfall.
Gold miners are opposed to the tax, saying it would leave some marginal mines unworkable.
They also are concerned share prices will suffer due to declines in the market-weighted average of gold companies hit with the levy at a time of low international prices.
ANZ Securities estimates that a two percent royalty would cause the market-weighted average of affected companies to decline 3.6 percent.
Though the industry has been profitable over the past 15 years, the government could not have picked a worse time to consider a royalty, Lalor said.
A strong Australian dollar agains the U.S. dollar had reduced the spot price of gold by A$100 an ounce over the last year, he said.
"Gold has been exempted from this type of tax for more than a century and this exemption has been one of the key factors in the survival of the industry through difficult times," he said.
Lalor is also managing director of Sons of Gwalia Ltd, one of Australia's largest gold mining companies.
